title: Nokia Had 40% of All Phones. Six Years Later, It Quit

scenes.narration: At the end of 2007, four out of every ten mobile phones sold on Earth were made by one company.

visual.subtitle: of all phones sold worldwide, Q4 2007

scenes.narration: That November, Forbes put it on the cover. One billion customers. Can anyone catch the cell phone king?

visual.title: Forbes cover, November 2007
visual.text: Nokia. One billion customers. Can anyone catch the cell phone king?

scenes.narration: Six years later, Nokia sold its entire phone business to Microsoft for five point four billion euros.
Nokia didn't lose to a better phone. It lost to a different idea of what a phone was.

visual.text:
It didn't lose to a better phone.
It lost to a different idea of what a phone was.

scenes.narration: This is Built and Broken. Episode two. Nokia.

visual.text: NOKIA
visual.subtitle: Built & Broken · Episode 2

scenes.narration: The story starts in 1865, in Finland, with a mining engineer named Fredrik Idestam and a mill that ground wood into pulp for paper.

visual.subtitle: Fredrik Idestam opens a pulp mill in Tampere, Finland

scenes.narration: He built a second mill near a small town on the Nokianvirta river. In 1871, the company took the town's name. Nokia.

visual.subtitle: The company takes the name of a river town: Nokia

scenes.narration: For the next century, Nokia was not a technology company. In 1967 it merged with the Finnish Rubber Works and the Finnish Cable Works.

visual.subtitle: Nokia merges with Finnish Rubber Works and Finnish Cable Works

scenes.narration: The new Nokia made paper, rubber boots, car tires, power cables, and later televisions and computers. It was a conglomerate. A bit of everything.

visual.text: A bit of everything
visual.subtitle: Paper · rubber boots · tyres · cables · TVs

scenes.narration: But inside the cable business was a small electronics division, and it started building radio telephones.

visual.text:
Inside the cable business:
a small electronics division

scenes.narration: In 1987 it released the Mobira Cityman, a brick-sized phone. Two years later, Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev was photographed in Helsinki using one to call Moscow.
In Finland, people nicknamed the phone the Gorba.

visual.text: "The Gorba"
visual.subtitle: Finland's nickname for the Cityman

scenes.narration: Then everything went wrong at once.

visual.text: Then everything went wrong at once.

scenes.narration: In 1988, Nokia's chairman, Kari Kairamo, the man who had pushed it into electronics, died by suicide.

visual.subtitle: Chairman Kari Kairamo dies

scenes.narration: In 1991, the Soviet Union collapsed, and Finland, which had traded heavily with it, fell into a deep recession.

visual.subtitle: The Soviet Union collapses. Finland falls into a deep recession.

scenes.narration: Nokia was losing money. One of its bank owners wanted out. And that year, the Swedish rival Ericsson held talks to buy Nokia.

visual.text: Ericsson holds talks to buy Nokia.

scenes.narration: The deal fell apart. Ericsson wanted the phones and the networks, but not the loss-making television business that came with them.
It may be the most important deal that never happened in the history of mobile phones.

visual.text:
The most important deal
that never happened

scenes.narration: In 1992, a new chief executive took over. Jorma Ollila. His plan was simple and brutal. Sell everything that is not telecoms.

visual.title: 1992 · Jorma Ollila becomes CEO
visual.text: Sell everything that is not telecoms.

scenes.narration: Paper, rubber, cables, televisions. All of it went. Nokia bet the company on one product.

visual.text: One product.
visual.subtitle: Paper, rubber, cables, TVs: all sold

scenes.narration: The timing was perfect. On the first of July 1991, the world's first call on a GSM network was made in Finland, on a Nokia phone.

visual.subtitle: The first GSM call, made in Finland on a Nokia phone

scenes.narration: GSM was the new digital standard for Europe, and soon most of the world. Nokia knew it better than almost anyone.

visual.text:
GSM: the digital standard
that went global

scenes.narration: In 1994 came the Nokia twenty-one ten, and with it a ringtone you can probably hear right now. The Nokia tune.

visual.text: Nokia 2110
visual.subtitle: 1994 · the first phone with the Nokia tune

scenes.narration: Nokia's phones were cheap to make, tough, easy to use, and they lasted for days on one charge. In 1998, Nokia passed Motorola to become the biggest phone maker in the world.

visual.subtitle: 1998: Nokia passes Motorola as the world's biggest phone maker

scenes.narration: In 2000, at the peak of the dot-com boom, Nokia was worth about three hundred and three billion euros, the most valuable company in Europe.

visual.subtitle: Peak market value, 2000: Europe's most valuable company

scenes.narration: For a country of five million people, it was enormous. At its peak, Nokia was about four percent of Finland's economy and around a fifth of its exports.

Then came the phones people still remember. The thirty-three ten in 2000. And the Nokia eleven hundred in 2003, which sold more than two hundred and fifty million units, one of the best-selling phones ever made.
scenes.note: 3310 figure (about 126 million) is the widely reported estimate; 1100 is 'over 250 million'.

scenes.narration: By the end of 2007, Nokia sold forty percent of all phones on the planet. One hundred and thirty three million in a single quarter.
Here is the part people get wrong. Nokia did not miss the smartphone.

visual.text: Nokia did not miss the smartphone.

scenes.narration: It practically invented it. In 1996 it launched the Nokia nine thousand Communicator, a phone that opened up into a keyboard with email and the web.

visual.subtitle: Nokia 9000 Communicator: email and web in your pocket

scenes.narration: Around 2004, according to a former Nokia engineer, a team built a prototype with a large touchscreen and internet access. Management decided it was too risky, and shelved it.

visual.title: c. 2004, as later reported by The New York Times
visual.text: A touchscreen, internet-ready prototype. Judged too risky. Shelved.

scenes.narration: And in 2007, Nokia's Symbian software ran on roughly six in ten smartphones in the world.

visual.subtitle: Symbian's share of smartphones, Q4 2007

scenes.narration: So what was the problem? Nokia was the best company in the world at building phones. Hardware. Factories. Supply chains. Dozens of models for every price and every market.

visual.text:
The best in the world
at building phones

scenes.narration: Software was something you put inside the phone. And Nokia kept score the old way. How many phones did we ship?
In January 2007, Apple announced the iPhone. A year and a half later, the first Android phone went on sale.
By Nokia's old scoreboard, nothing looked wrong. It was still selling more phones than anyone.

visual.text:
By the old scoreboard,
nothing looked wrong.

scenes.narration: But the new scoreboard was apps, touchscreens, and developers. And there, Symbian was falling fast. Forty seven percent of smartphones in 2009. Thirty eight in 2010. Under four percent by 2012.
In September 2010, Nokia hired a new chief executive from Microsoft. Stephen Elop.

visual.subtitle: Stephen Elop, a Microsoft executive, becomes Nokia's CEO

scenes.narration: In February 2011, an internal memo from Elop leaked. He told staff that Nokia was standing on a burning platform.

visual.title: Stephen Elop, internal memo, February 2011
visual.text: We are standing on a burning platform.

scenes.narration: Days later, Nokia announced it would abandon Symbian and switch to Microsoft's Windows Phone. Its shares fell fourteen percent that day.

visual.subtitle: Nokia's share price on 11 February 2011

scenes.narration: Here's the trap. Nokia had announced the end of its old phones before the new ones were ready. Why would anyone buy a Symbian phone now?

visual.text:
It announced the end of its old phones
before the new ones were ready.

scenes.narration: The Lumia phones that followed were well reviewed, but Windows Phone never caught up with the apps on iPhone and Android. By the third quarter of 2012, Nokia had three and a half percent of the smartphone market.

visual.subtitle: Nokia's smartphone market share, Q3 2012

scenes.narration: In September 2013, Microsoft agreed to buy Nokia's phone business for five point four four billion euros. About thirty two thousand people moved to Microsoft.
It didn't work. In 2015, Microsoft wrote off seven point six billion dollars on the deal and announced seven thousand eight hundred job cuts, mostly in phones.
But this is where Nokia's story is different from Kodak's.

visual.text:
Where Nokia's story
is different from Kodak's

scenes.narration: Nokia didn't die. It did what Jorma Ollila did in 1992. It cut down to the thing it was still best at, the networks that carry the calls, and in 2016 it bought the French rival Alcatel-Lucent.
Today, Nokia builds the equipment behind mobile networks around the world. The name on the phones is licensed to another company.

visual.text:
Nokia still builds the networks.
The phones carry its name under licence.

scenes.narration: Kodak lost because it protected its profits. Nokia lost because it measured the wrong thing.
It counted phones shipped, while the market started counting apps, developers, and what you could do with the screen.

visual.text:
It counted phones.
The market counted what the phone could do.

scenes.narration: Being the best at the old game is not the same as winning the new one. And sometimes, being the best at the old game is exactly what stops you from playing the new one.

visual.text:
Being the best at the old game
can stop you playing the new one.

scenes.narration: This has been Built and Broken. If you want the next story of a giant that saw the future and still fell, subscribe.
